extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political philosophy; anyone studying social-contract theory and the origin/limits of government
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts principles about how political societies are legitimately formed, what ends they serve, and the rightful extent and forms of legislative power according to classical social‑contract theory (Lockean line). Useful for evaluating claims about political legitimacy, consent, and limits on government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Origin of political society depends on consent
rubrics_metrics.description: The beginning of politic society depends upon the consent of the individuals, to join into, and make one society; who, when they are thus incorporated, might set up what form of government they thought fit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consent (explicit or tacit) is the foundation of legitimate government; history shows peaceful beginnings of governments laid in consent rather than by paternal right or divine claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paternal authority is not the foundation of government
rubrics_metrics.description: Though fathers rule their children in childhood, paternal power is not the original right of dominion nor the foundation of monarchy; people did not generally conceive monarchy to be iure divino or an extension of paternal power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains and rejects the mistaken inference that government by one (monarchy) derives legitimacy from the father's authority; historical multiplicity of petty kingdoms refutes a single paternal-based universal sovereignty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Early preference for monarchy explained by familiarity and military need
rubrics_metrics.description: People naturally ran into monarchy because they had been accustomed from childhood to the rule of one man (the father) and because in early societies the need was chiefly defence against foreign force, making a single commander (general) most suitable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monarchy's appeal is practical and situational (simplicity, a single leader for war), not necessarily normative justification for absolute power. Examples include kings as generals among American Indians and early Israelites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kingly authority often limited in peace; war concentrates command in one
rubrics_metrics.description: Kings, while commanding absolutely in war, commonly exercise very little dominion at home and have but very moderate sovereignty; the resolution of peace and war often lies with the people or a council.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical examples (Israelite judges and early kings like Jephtha, Saul, David) show the military role distinct from domestic legislative or judicial authority—an argument against attributing unlimited domestic power to kings.

rubrics_metrics.name: People may form governments by uniting families or delegating to a single person
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether by continuation of a father's authority within a growing family or by several families uniting for mutual defence, people have put the rule into a single person's hands 'for the public good and safety'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The form (one, few, or many) depends on how the community places the supreme power; initial entrustment of authority is for public safety and preservation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to separate and form new commonwealths
rubrics_metrics.description: There are frequent historical examples of men withdrawing obedience from jurisdictions they were born under and setting up new governments; this shows people born under a government are not necessarily bound perpetually by it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to rebut the claim that being born subject to a government deprives one of liberty to found a new government; multiplicity of petty commonwealths historically confirms this liberty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Being born under a government does not bind one by ancestral compact
rubrics_metrics.description: A son, when a man, is as free as the father; no act of the father can give away the liberty of the son; children are not thereby born subjects of any country or government permanently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Governments' own practices (e.g., admission procedures for denizens) demonstrate children are not automatic subjects; membership requires admission/consent once at age of discretion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between express and tacit consent
rubrics_metrics.description: Express consent clearly makes a man a member of a society; the difficulty is what shall be looked upon as tacit consent, and how far it binds a person where he has made no expressions at all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text analyzes what counts as sufficient tacit consent and sets boundaries for its application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possession/enjoyment implies tacit consent
rubrics_metrics.description: Every man that hath any possessions, or enjoyment, of any part of the dominions of any government, doth thereby give his tacit consent, and is as far forth obliged to obedience to the laws of that government, during such enjoyment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applies to land (even ephemeral lodging) or travelling on highways; the obligation begins and ends with the enjoyment—one may quit the possession and thereby leave the obligation if it was only tacit consent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local enjoyment/confined protection does not make one a perpetual member
rubrics_metrics.description: Submitting to the laws, living quietly, and enjoying privileges under them makes not a man a member of that society; foreigners living under another government and enjoying protection are not thereby made subjects unless they enter by positive engagement and express promise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes mere temporary/local obligation (e.g., while enjoying protection) from actual incorporation into the commonwealth, which requires explicit commitment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chief end of political society: preservation of property
rubrics_metrics.description: The great and chief end, therefore, of men’s uniting into commonwealths, and putting themselves under government, is the preservation of their property (lives, liberties and estates).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provides the standard by which governments and laws should be judged: do they secure life, liberty, and estate?

rubrics_metrics.name: Three defects in the state of nature justifying government
rubrics_metrics.description: In the state of nature there wants (1) an established, settled, known law received by common consent; (2) a known and indifferent judge; (3) power to back and support sentences when right and to give them due execution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These defects—uncertain law, partial adjudicators, and lack of enforcement—are the practical reasons men quit the state of nature for government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Powers given up when entering society: regulation of conduct and punishment
rubrics_metrics.description: A man in the state of nature has (1) power to do whatsoever he thinks fit for preservation (within the law of nature) and (2) the power to punish crimes; both are given up when he joins a particular political society and incorporates into a commonwealth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The first power is regulated by laws made by the society; the second (punishment) is wholly given up and engaged to the executive power as the law of the society requires.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative power established by society is the supreme political power
rubrics_metrics.description: The first and fundamental positive law of all commonwealths is the establishing of the legislative power; this legislative is not only the supreme power of the commonwealth but derives its force from the consent of the society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No edict by any other body has the force of a law without sanction from the legislative that the community chose; obedience ultimately terminates in this supreme power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative power is limited by the public good and the law of nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Though supreme, the legislative is not, nor can it possibly be, absolutely arbitrary over the lives and fortunes of the people; its power is limited to the public good, and cannot rightfully destroy, enslave, or designedly impoverish the subjects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No one can transfer to another more power than he has in himself; human laws must conform to the law of nature and the preservation of mankind, which remain an eternal rule for legislators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laws should be established, promulgated, and not extemporary decrees
rubrics_metrics.description: Whoever has the legislative or supreme power of any commonwealth is bound to govern by established standing laws, promulgated and known to the people, and not by extemporary decrees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rule of law requirement: laws must be known and stable so individuals can regulate their conduct; arbitrary or secret rules violate the social contract's purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form of government defined by location of supreme/legislative power
rubrics_metrics.description: If the majority employ the whole power in making laws and executing them the form is a democracy; if placed in few select men it is an oligarchy; if in one man it is a monarchy; communities may also make compounded or mixed forms depending on how supreme power is placed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form is functionally determined by where legislative power is vested and whether it's for life, heredity, election, or temporary delegation—allowing for mixed/compound governments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligations of the subject derived from consent to the legislative, not from oaths to other powers
rubrics_metrics.description: All obedience which by any solemn ties one can be obliged to pay ultimately terminates in the supreme power; no oaths to any foreign or subordinate power can discharge members from obedience to the legislative acting pursuant to their trust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes that allegiance is owed to the community's legislative authority established by consent; conflicting private or foreign obligations do not supersede this.
